subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 51-year-old woman with primary biliary cholangitis presents with jaundice, pruritus, and steatorrhea. Over the past 2 weeks she has developed extensive ecchymoses on her arms and legs after minor trauma. Laboratory studies show a prothrombin time of 21 seconds, an activated partial thromboplastin time of 48 seconds, normal platelets, and a normal bleeding time.
question: Deficiency of which of the following proteins best explains her coagulopathy?
explanation_correct: Vitamin K is the cofactor for the epoxide reductase cycle that regenerates reduced vitamin K, which a gamma-carboxylase uses to carboxylate glutamate residues on factors II, VII, IX, and X and on proteins C and S. Cholestasis impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption, so both procoagulant factors and the vitamin K-dependent anticoagulant protein C are depleted, prolonging the PT and aPTT; parenteral vitamin K corrects the abnormality if the liver synthetic capacity is intact.

explanation_incorrect.A: Factor VIII is synthesized in endothelial cells and is not vitamin K dependent, so its deficiency (hemophilia A) prolongs only the aPTT.
explanation_incorrect.B: Factor V is a cofactor in the common pathway but does not undergo vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation, so it is unaffected by fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fibrinogen is not vitamin K dependent and would be normal here; its deficiency would prolong thrombin and reptilase times.
explanation_incorrect.E: von Willebrand factor mediates platelet adhesion and is not a vitamin K-dependent protein, so its deficiency prolongs the bleeding time rather than the PT.

educationalObjective: Vitamin K-dependent proteins include factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S, and their deficiency from fat malabsorption prolongs both the PT and aPTT.
